purpose: Clobazam is mainly used to help control seizures, especially in people with a condition called Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. It can also sometimes be used to help with anxiety. It works alongside other seizure medications to give better control.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical called GABA to calm down electrical activity. Clobazam boosts the effect of GABA, which helps quiet the overactive brain signals that cause seizures. Think of it like turning down the volume on a radio that is playing too loud.
common_side_effects: Feeling sleepy or drowsy, drooling, trouble with coordination or balance, feeling agitated or aggressive (especially in children), constipation, and changes in appetite. Most of these tend to improve after your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly — it must be tapered slowly or it can cause withdrawal seizures or other serious problems. It can cause breathing problems, especially if combined with opioid pain medicines, alcohol, or other sedatives. It may be habit-forming with long-term use. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until you know how it affects you. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
typical_dosing: For adults and children over 30 kg, dosing usually starts at 5–10 mg per day and may be gradually increased up to 40 mg per day, split into two doses. For smaller children (under 30 kg), doses are lower, typically starting at 5 mg per day. Your doctor will adjust your dose slowly to find what works best for you.
